papers.title: Ill-Posedness of the 2D Euler Equations in a Logarithmically Refined Critical Sobolev Space
papers.authors: Elaine Cozzi, Nicholas Harrison, and Zachary Radke
papers.description: Strong ill-posedness persists under logarithmic refinements of the critical H² velocity norm, up to the exponent α = 1/2.

idea.text: Can a little extra smoothness prevent instability?

A logarithmic weight strengthens the critical Sobolev norm without requiring an additional positive power of differentiability. This paper asks whether that small improvement restores control of the Euler evolution.

results.text: The paper establishes strong ill-posedness for 2D Euler in the logarithmically refined critical spaces H²,α for α ≤ 1/2. Consult the paper for the full hypotheses and precise norm-inflation formulation.

papers.title: Well-Posedness for the Euler Equations in Function Spaces of Generalized Smoothness
papers.description: Existence and well-posedness at critical smoothness with additional slowly varying weights, together with a continuation criterion and two-dimensional global existence.

idea.text: Measuring smoothness between the usual scales
Slowly varying weights distinguish functions that have the same critical differentiability exponent. They provide finer control than the exponent alone.

results.text: For generalized Besov and Triebel–Lizorkin spaces at s = d/p + 1, sufficiently fast growth of the slowly varying weight yields local solutions under the stated parameter assumptions. A Beale–Kato–Majda-type continuation criterion gives global existence in two dimensions.

proof.text: Control the equation one frequency scale at a time.
Use Littlewood–Paley decompositions to track the slowly varying weights across frequency scales.
proof.title: Resolve the frequency scales

proof.text: Establish weighted product and commutator bounds for the transport nonlinearity.
proof.title: Estimate the nonlinear interactions

proof.text: Use the resulting a priori estimates to construct local solutions, then apply the continuation criterion in two dimensions.
proof.title: Construct and continue solutions

papers.title: Local Existence for the 2D Euler Equations in a Critical Sobolev Space
papers.description: Short-time existence with vorticity in W²,¹(ℝ²), with global persistence of that regularity under an additional Dini continuity assumption.

idea.text: What happens at the L¹ endpoint?
The endpoint W²,¹ vorticity space requires estimates that do not follow from the usual Lᵖ theory for p > 1.

results.text: Local existence and a conditional global result

Initial vorticity in W²,¹(ℝ²) admits a short-time solution retaining this regularity. If the initial vorticity is also Dini continuous, the regularity persists globally. The global statement needs this additional assumption.

proof.text: Use Lorentz-space estimates to bound the velocity gradient and close the a priori inequality.
proof.title: Control the velocity gradient

proof.text: Approximate by smooth solutions and obtain uniform W²,¹ bounds. Address equiintegrability and tightness when taking limits in L¹.
proof.title: Pass to a weak solution

proof.text: Use the additional modulus of continuity to control the velocity gradient and continue the regularity for all time.
proof.title: Use Dini continuity for global control

about: Away from mathematics, I enjoy rock climbing, spending time outdoors, and looking for mushrooms. This is a place for occasional photographs and notes from outside the office.
researchIntro: My research connects the analysis of nonlinear PDEs with the mechanisms that drive concentration, transport, and loss of regularity.
teachingIntro: Models become more memorable when you can experiment with them. My teaching connects mathematical ideas with concrete questions, computation, and applications.

idea.text: A tiny change can hide a large difference.
SQG describes a scalar carried by a fluid whose velocity is determined by that same scalar. This feedback makes its mathematical behavior subtle.
Two initial states can be arbitrarily close in a norm measuring their derivatives, yet their smooth solutions can later be arbitrarily far apart in that norm.
What you measure matters: the instability concerns derivatives in L¹. It does not assert that the temperature itself becomes arbitrarily large.
The W³,¹ norm controls the velocity gradient. That useful estimate still does not close the highest-order derivative estimate.

results.text: Norm inflation near a smooth background

Fix a nonconstant smooth, compactly supported background solution and a positive target time τ within its smooth lifespan. For every ε, M > 0 and integer k ≥ 3, a smooth compactly supported perturbation can be chosen with initial Wᵏ,¹ distance below ε and distance at τ above M. Its solution exists through τ.
Instantaneous loss of bounded norm control
Arbitrarily close to each nonconstant smooth compactly supported datum, there is compactly supported Wᵏ,¹ data whose corresponding solution satisfies
ess sup_{0<t<T′} ‖θ(t)‖_{Wᵏ,¹} = ∞   for every 0 < T′ ≤ T.
This essential-supremum statement does not assert that the norm is infinite at every positive time. See Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 for the precise formulation.

proof.text: The perturbation creates a velocity that moves the background scalar. After local approximation and a change of coordinates, this gives a nonconstant multiplier homogeneous of degree zero.

proof.title: 1. Find an amplifying profile
proof.text: The Bonami–Poornima theorem supplies a profile with a large multiplier response relative to the initial derivative norm.

proof.title: 2. Dilute the nonlinear error
proof.text: Distributing the perturbation among many smaller packets controls self-interaction while preserving the desired amplification.

proof.title: 3. Concentrate the packets
proof.text: A sufficiently small spatial scale controls the errors from approximating the background flow and scalar gradient.

proof.title: 4. Pass to a single limiting datum
proof.text: Iterated norm inflation and stability in an auxiliary Sobolev–Lorentz solution class yield one datum with unbounded norm control on every initial time interval.
